turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, this login timed out on me again. Sam, and you're Riley, yeah? What brings you in, Sam?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): My heart keeps racing, and I get short of breath with it. It's been freaking me out. Is that something dangerous?
[SEG0003] person_1 (DOCTOR): Racing and breathless, okay. When did it start?
[SEG0004] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): About two months. It really kicked up once he started the new marketing job. We share the apartment, so I'm the one awake for it.
[SEG0005] person_2 (PATIENT): No, that's not two months. I thought three months for a second... no, six weeks. The job started six weeks ago, and that's when the heart thing started.
[SEG0006] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sorry, say the timing one more time? I was clicking the wrong tab.
[SEG0007] person_2 (PATIENT): Six weeks. Not two months and not three. Six weeks.
[SEG0008] person_1 (DOCTOR): Alright. When does it actually happen?
[SEG0009] person_2 (PATIENT): Mostly at night, lying in bed. And right before an exam or a big work meeting. I'm not stressed, though. I do fine under pressure, so don't write it up as anxiety.
[SEG0010] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He wakes me up almost every night. Heart pounding, breathing fast, just lying there on his back.

[SEG0011] person_2 (PATIENT): Not every night. It's like four nights a week. And I'm not panting just lying around, it comes with the pounding. It lasts an hour... no, more like ten minutes, then it eases off.
[SEG0012] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any chest pain with those episodes?
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): I've got a stats exam Thursday and a client pitch Friday, and I keep thinking I should cancel, because what if I pass out in front of everybody?
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): I caught the exam. I still need the chest pain piece. Pain in your chest, yes or no?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No chest pain. I just feel it beating.
[SEG0016] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He does grab at his chest, though. He told me last week it feels tight, like a band.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): I didn't say that. I put my hand there so I can feel the beat, not because it's tight. There is no tightness.
[SEG0018] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any fainting, or feeling like you're about to faint?
[SEG0019] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't passed out. I get scared I might, but I don't actually get lightheaded enough to drop. Is almost-scared the same as almost-fainting? I don't think so.
[SEG0020] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not the same. How much caffeine are you taking in? Coffee, energy drinks?
[SEG0021] person_2 (PATIENT): Coffee, like eight cups a day... well, not eight. More like five. And energy drinks, two... actually three Red Bulls, most days. Is that insane?
[SEG0022] person_1 (DOCTOR): Five coffees and three Red Bulls? Say it again, this fan is louder than you are.
[SEG0023] person_2 (PATIENT): Five coffees, three Red Bulls. Could that give me a heart attack at twenty-four? Be honest.
[SEG0024] person_1 (DOCTOR): It can make your heart race. A heart attack at twenty-four would be very unusual, which is why we still check. Do you smoke or vape anything?
[SEG0025] person_2 (PATIENT): I vape. Nicotine. I've been doing it for two years... wait, no, I started last fall, so about eight months. Does nicotine do this too?
[SEG0026] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): All day. Between classes and at his desk, that thing is in his hand.
[SEG0027] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah, pretty much through the day. I'm not quitting this afternoon if that's where you're headed. Can vaping alone cause palpitations?
[SEG0028] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nicotine can, yes. I'd like you to cut back, ideally stop, and we'll get specific in a minute. Any medicines, prescribed or over the counter?
[SEG0029] person_2 (PATIENT): Nothing regular. My roommate takes propranolol for stage fright and I thought about borrowing one, but I never actually took it. Should I have?
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): No, don't take someone else's propranolol. Any allergies to medicines?
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): No. None that I know of. Would an allergy even look like a racing heart?
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not typically like this. Family history, heart disease or thyroid problems?
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): My mom has hyperthyroidism. Graves, I think. She takes a pill for it. Is this genetic? Am I going to end up on the same medicine?
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not automatically, but it makes me want labs. Let me listen. Heart rhythm is regular, a bit quick, no murmur. Lungs are clear.
[SEG0035] person_1 (DOCTOR): Pulse is ninety... no, the readout says one-ten. Blood pressure is one-eighteen over seventy-six. Oxygen is ninety-nine percent.
[SEG0036] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He's lost weight too. Like ten pounds since the job started. He won't admit it.

[SEG0037] person_2 (PATIENT): I haven't been trying to lose weight, and I don't think it's ten pounds. My jeans fit the same. Maybe a couple pounds, I don't know. Why, is weight loss the thyroid thing?
[SEG0038] person_1 (DOCTOR): Weight loss is unclear, we'll see. Any diarrhea, feeling hot all the time, or shaking in your hands?
[SEG0039] person_2 (PATIENT): No diarrhea. I feel warm at night, but I think that's just the racing. My hands don't shake except when an episode hits. If it's thyroid, is that fixable?
[SEG0040] person_1 (DOCTOR): Usually, yes, if that's even what this is. First plan, I'm going to order a twenty-four hour Holter so we can catch an episode on a recording.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): A Holter? Do I wear that to my exam? What if it beeps in the middle of the pitch? And how soon will you know if my heart is okay?
[SEG0042] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He also barely sleeps, maybe four hours. And he says he's not anxious, but he paces the kitchen before every meeting.
[SEG0043] person_2 (PATIENT): I sleep fine, like six hours. I don't pace. I stand there and review my notes. I'm not an anxious person, I keep telling people that.
[SEG0044] person_1 (DOCTOR): Hold on, I'm pulling up your mom's note in the chart, or trying to. Actually I'm changing the plan. Skip the Holter for now.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): My working thought is the caffeine and the vape, plus that pre-meeting adrenaline, even if you hate the stress label. I still can't rule out your thyroid or a rhythm problem. We'll do an ECG today and blood for TSH and free T4. If those are normal and this keeps going, then we revisit a monitor.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): Does the ECG hurt? How many needles is the thyroid test? If the TSH comes back high, does that mean I have Graves?

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): ECG is stickers, no pain. One needle, both tests from the same tube. A high TSH usually means underactive, not Graves. Graves tends to run a low TSH. We look at the numbers before anyone mentions pills.
[SEG0048] person_2 (PATIENT): Okay. There was a poster in the hall about breathing. Is that actually useful, or is it just a poster?
[SEG0049] person_1 (DOCTOR): It's useful for this. When it starts, breathe in for four counts and out for six, a few minutes. It won't fix a thyroid problem, but it can slow the racing feeling.
[SEG0050] person_2 (PATIENT): So do I cut coffee all the way out? And the Red Bulls? Can I still vape if I'm doing the breathing thing?

[SEG0051] person_1 (DOCTOR): Drop the energy drinks completely. Cut coffee to one cup in the morning. I'd rather you stop vaping. If you can't today, don't vape in the hour before bed or before those meetings.
[SEG0052] person_2 (PATIENT): One cup is going to hurt. What if I get a headache from stopping? Is that dangerous, or am I being dramatic?
[SEG0053] person_1 (DOCTOR): A caffeine withdrawal headache is common and not dangerous. Water, and plain acetaminophen if you need it. Don't grab the kind with caffeine already in it.
[SEG0054] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'll move the Red Bulls out of the fridge. And I'll remind him to do the breathing instead of reaching for the vape.
[SEG0055] person_2 (PATIENT): You don't have to hide stuff, Riley. I'll cut them. I just need to know this isn't going to kill me before Thursday. Should I still sit the exam?

[SEG0056] person_1 (DOCTOR): Nothing here says you're about to die, and yes, sit the exam. Get the ECG before you leave today and the labs downstairs. I'll see you back in three weeks with the results. If you faint, get real chest pain, or the breathing gets worse while you're just resting, go to the ER and don't wait on me.

features: self_correction: a speaker states a number, drug name or duration and then corrects it in the same turn or later ('seventy-five... no, hundred and fifty'). The label holds only the corrected value.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.
patient_answers_other_question: the patient answers a different question than the one asked, and the doctor repeats or lets it go.
spec.doctor_style: distracted by the computer, asks for repeats
